lessons.title: Test Automation - 1
lessons.lesson_objective: *Understand the core concepts of AI and how it applies to everyday workflows.

slides.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to computer systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence — recognizing patterns, making decisions, and learning from experience.

Core AI techniques include:

  • Machine Learning — Systems that improve by learning from data.
  • Natural Language Processing — Machines that read and generate human language.
  • Computer Vision — Machines that interpret images and video.
  • Robotic Process Automation — Software that mimics human actions on digital systems.

slides.question_body: A hospital wants to automatically flag X-ray images showing signs of abnormality. Which AI technique is best suited for this task?

options.label: A
options.feedback: NLP works with text and speech, not images.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct. Computer Vision analyzes images — exactly what is needed to scan X-rays.

options.label: C
options.feedback: RPA automates repetitive digital tasks. It cannot interpret image content.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Scheduled Automation runs tasks on a timer. It has no ability to interpret visual data.

slides.correct_feedback: Well done. Computer Vision is the right tool whenever the input is an image or video.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Think about what type of data is being analyzed. X-rays are images — the technique needs to interpret visual content.

slides.question_body: AI and automation are designed to completely replace human workers across all roles, including creative, strategic, and interpersonal positions.
slides.correct_feedback: Correct. AI augments human work rather than replacing it entirely. Creative judgment, empathy, and strategy remain distinctly human strengths.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Incorrect. AI handles repetitive and rule-based tasks well but cannot replicate human emotional intelligence or strategic thinking.

slides.question_body: Match each AI technique to the task it is best designed to handle.

options.label: A
options.match: Predicting customer churn from historical purchase data

options.label: B
options.match: Summarizing a contract into key bullet points

options.label: C
options.match: Detecting defective products on a manufacturing line via camera

options.label: D
options.match: Copying invoice data from email into an accounting system

slides.correct_feedback: Well done. Each technique has a distinct strength — matching it to the right task is the first step in building an effective AI solution.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the four core AI techniques. Each is defined by the type of input it processes.

slides.question_body: Sort each application into the correct category based on whether it is a current AI capability or not yet reliably possible.

items.label: A
items.text: Transcribing spoken meetings into searchable text

items.label: B
items.text: Fully replacing a doctor's clinical judgment in all diagnoses

items.label: C
items.text: Detecting fraud across millions of transactions per second

items.label: D
items.text: Forming genuine emotional relationships with users

slides.correct_feedback: Great work. Understanding what AI can reliably do today helps teams set realistic expectations.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review current AI capabilities. Pattern recognition and language generation are well established. Genuine empathy and clinical judgment still require humans.

lessons.title: Test Automation - 2
lessons.lesson_objective: *Identify how automation tools are applied to real business workflows.

slides.content:
Automation tools connect software systems and trigger actions based on defined rules. When a condition is met the tool executes the next step without human involvement.

The four core automation patterns are:

  • Trigger-Action — A specific event starts a predefined workflow.
  • Scheduled Automation — A task runs on a fixed schedule.
  • Conditional Logic — The workflow branches based on data values.
  • API Integration — Two systems share data automatically.

slides.question_body: Every Friday at 6 AM a script runs automatically and sends each department head a summary of the week's open support tickets. No one manually starts this process. Which automation pattern does this represent?
slides.correct_feedback: Correct. Scheduled Automation runs tasks at defined times without any triggering event.
slides.incorrect_feedback: The key is what starts the workflow — a fixed time schedule, not an event or condition.

slides.question_body: Once a workflow is automated it becomes completely error-free, since machines do not make the kinds of mistakes that humans do.

options.label: A
options.feedback: This is a myth. Automations can fail when APIs change, data is malformed, or configurations drift.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct. Automations reduce human error but introduce their own failure modes. Monitoring is essential.

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. Automations reduce human error but require ongoing monitoring to catch silent failures.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Automations can fail when connected systems change. They are not inherently error-free.

slides.question_body: Match each business scenario to the automation pattern it best represents.

options.label: A
options.text: New order submitted — confirmation email sent immediately

options.label: B
options.text: Database backup runs every night at 2 AM

options.label: C
options.text: Urgent ticket routed to senior agent; standard ticket to normal queue

options.label: D
options.text: CRM updates instantly when a sale closes in billing

slides.correct_feedback: Excellent. Recognizing which pattern fits a scenario is the first step in designing an effective workflow.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the four automation patterns. Each is defined by what starts the workflow and what logic decides the next step.

slides.question_body: Fill in the missing terms to complete this automation project brief.
slides.story_body: This automation will use a [[trigger]] to start when a customer submits a support request. The system will apply [[conditional logic]] to route tickets by priority. High-priority tickets go to [[senior agents]] while standard tickets enter the normal queue. All data syncs to our CRM via [[API integration]] in real time. The workflow will be tested in a [[staging environment]] before going live.
slides.correct_feedback: Well done. A clear automation brief aligns stakeholders before any build work begins.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the four automation patterns. Each blank represents a concept covered in this lesson.

slides.slide_name: Which Automation Would You Build First?
slides.question_body: Your team has budget to build one automation this quarter. Which would you prioritize?

choices.text: Automated onboarding emails when a new user signs up
Scheduled weekly report delivered to leadership automatically
Support ticket routing based on urgency and topic
Real-time CRM sync when a deal closes in billing

slides.feedback: All four are strong candidates. The right choice depends on where your team loses the most time today.

lessons.title: Test Automation - 3
lessons.lesson_objective: *Evaluate AI tools and plan a responsible, effective implementation.

slides.content:
Choosing the right AI tool requires a structured evaluation process. The wrong tool wastes budget. The right tool compounds in value over time.

Key evaluation criteria:

  • Fit for Purpose — Does the tool solve your specific problem?
  • Integration — Does it connect with your existing systems?
  • Scalability — Can it grow without dramatic cost increases?
  • Security — How does the vendor handle your data?
  • Support — Who owns the fix when something breaks?

Start with a narrow pilot. One workflow, one team, one tool. Measure before expanding.

slides.question_body: A company wants to deploy an AI writing assistant to all 200 employees immediately. A consultant recommends a 10-person pilot in one department first. What is the primary reason for the recommendation?

options.label: A
options.text: A pilot requires no vendor contract and costs less

options.label: B
options.text: A pilot limits risk and generates real data before full rollout

options.label: C
options.text: A pilot prevents employees from learning the tool too quickly

options.label: D
options.text: A pilot is legally required for AI deployments over 50 users

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. Pilots surface integration issues and adoption challenges before they affect the whole organization.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the implementation best practices. The value of a pilot is risk reduction and real-world learning.

slides.question_body: When an AI tool produces harmful or misleading output, the organization that deployed it is responsible — even if the error originated in the vendor's underlying model.
slides.correct_feedback: Right. Organizations are accountable for how they deploy AI. Vendor agreements typically disclaim liability for outputs.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Actually this is correct. The organization deploying the AI owns responsibility for its outputs.

slides.question_body: Sort each activity into the correct phase of an AI tool rollout.

items.label: A
items.text: Define the specific problem the AI tool will solve

items.label: B
items.text: Collect feedback from pilot users on what is working

items.label: C
items.text: Establish a process for monitoring ongoing AI output quality

items.label: D
items.text: Select a vendor and negotiate contract terms

slides.correct_feedback: Well done. A structured rollout with clear phases reduces failed implementations.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the three rollout phases. Problem definition and vendor selection happen before any user touches the tool.

slides.question_body: Fill in the missing terms to complete this AI implementation plan summary.
slides.story_body: We will begin with a [[pilot program]] involving one team and one workflow. Success will be measured by tracking [[time saved]] versus our manual baseline. Before launch we will conduct a [[security review]] to verify the vendor meets our compliance requirements. Pilot users will receive [[training]] before the tool goes live. After the pilot we will [[iterate]] on the configuration before expanding to the full organization.
slides.correct_feedback: Well done. This plan reflects the structured approach that separates successful AI implementations from ones that fail.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the implementation best practices. Each blank reflects a required step in responsible AI deployment.

slides.slide_name: Which Tool Would You Evaluate First?
slides.question_body: Your organization is ready to evaluate its first AI tool. Which category would you prioritize?

choices.text: AI writing assistant for content and communications
Automated document processing and data entry

slides.feedback: There is no universally correct answer. The right first tool depends on where your team spends the most time on low-value work.
